nodes.label: Daniel Roche
nodes.date_label: Le Peuple de Paris (1981) · La Culture des apparences (1989) · Histoire des choses banales (1997)
nodes.description: Historian of Enlightenment France whose studies of clothing, possessions and everyday practices connected material culture to social differentiation. In dialogue with Gil Bartholeyns, Roche insists that representations require attention to their production, circulation and unequal reception. His consumption history examines changing needs and access to goods rather than treating objects as isolated curiosities.

nodes.label: Linda Gordon
nodes.date_label: Heroes of Their Own Lives (1988) · Pitied But Not Entitled (1994) · The Great Arizona Orphan Abduction (1999)
nodes.description: Historian of gender, social policy and unequal power in American families. Gordon’s autobiographical account links her turn to women’s history with the women’s liberation movement. Her research on welfare and family violence treats domestic relations as public and political, while The Great Arizona Orphan Abduction reconstructs the interaction of race, family claims and local power through a tightly focused narrative.

nodes.label: David Armitage
nodes.date_label: The Ideological Origins of the British Empire (2000) · The Declaration of Independence: A Global History (2007) · Foundations of Modern International Thought (2013)
nodes.description: Intellectual and international historian who studies political concepts through their changing imperial and global settings. Armitage’s introduction to The Ideological Origins of the British Empire reconnects state formation in Britain and Ireland with empire and challenges a rigid domestic/overseas separation. His Atlantic research traces how a British imperial community was articulated, rather than assuming that it existed unchanged.

nodes.label: John Brewer
nodes.date_label: The Sinews of Power (1989) · Consumption and the World of Goods (coeditor Roy Porter) (1993) · The Pleasures of the Imagination (1997)
nodes.description: Historian of eighteenth-century Britain whose work crosses state finance, cultural production and consumption. In his2026 memoir Brewer explains that The Sinews of Power challenged the idea of a weak British state while investigating resistance and special interests within fiscal expansion. He resists fixed disciplinary labels and treats literature and the arts as connected historical practices rather than autonomous masterpieces.

nodes.label: Alan Taylor
nodes.date_label: American Colonies (2001) · The Divided Ground (2006) · The Civil War of1812 (2010)
nodes.description: Historian of early North America whose continental approach unsettles self-contained national narratives. Taylor’s interview on American Civil Wars connects conflicts in the United States,Mexico and Canada through intervention,union and political economy. His work also treats British and American sovereignty as incomplete projects rather than inevitable outcomes of a single national revolution.

nodes.label: Geoff Eley
nodes.date_label: Forging Democracy (2002) · A Crooked Line (2005) · Nazism as Fascism (2013)
nodes.description: Historian of modern Europe and historiography whose writing reconsiders the relation between social and cultural history. Jaume Aurell reads A Crooked Line as a deliberate use of intellectual autobiography to interpret the cultural turn and its political conditions. This plural approach does not require historians to abandon social questions when studying meaning, nor does Eley’s path stand for every national historiography.

nodes.label: Mark Mazower
nodes.date_label: Dark Continent (1998) · Hitler’s Empire (2008) · No Enchanted Palace (2009)
nodes.description: Historian of modern Europe and international order who questions celebratory accounts of liberal progress. Glenda Sluga’s reading of No Enchanted Palace identifies the imperial and racial assumptions carried into twentieth-century international institutions. Mazower’s later interview links global institutions to the power and interests of states, preserving the tension between universal claims and unequal political authority.

nodes.label: Gérard Noiriel
nodes.date_label: Les Ouvriers dans la société française (1986) · Le Creuset français (1988) · Introduction à la socio-histoire (2006)
nodes.description: Historian of labour,immigration and state classification whose socio-history follows relationships among identifiable people. In interviews Noiriel presents socio-history as a collective venture rather than a personal school,and treats immigration categories as historically constructed through public language and administrative power. His method connects sociology to archival history while distinguishing explanation from political judgment.

nodes.label: Robin D. G Kelley
nodes.date_label: Hammer and Hoe (1990) · Race Rebels (1994) · Freedom Dreams (2002)
nodes.description: Historian of Black labour,political culture and radical imagination. In his2022 retrospective Kelley explains Freedom Dreams as a history of movements’ visions rather than a programme predicting future victories. He places collective imagining within struggles on the ground,showing why cultural practices and aspirations matter alongside organizations and campaigns. His accounts do not assign every movement a common strategy.

nodes.label: Tony Judt
nodes.date_label: Past Imperfect (1992) · The Burden of Responsibility (1998) · Postwar (2005)
nodes.description: Historian of modern Europe whose Postwar joins Eastern and Western experiences through war’s consequences,political reconstruction and contested memory. In his interview with Donald Yerxa,Judt argues that selective forgetting enabled postwar national narratives and that European integration emerged through national interests. These are his interpretations,with differences across societies retained rather than a single story of inevitable liberal success.

edges.evidence_note: David Blackburn’s2012 interview report, paragraphs on states and international bodies; source mediation explicit.

edges.evidence_note: Own2022 retrospective explicitly says Freedom Dreams was neither roadmap nor prediction; particular movements rather than a universal programme.

edges.relationship: Kelley treats collective imagination as a practice generated within political struggle and cultural life.
edges.evidence_note: Own2022 opening distinguishes sustained visions from narrow measures of campaign success; cultural imagination is not detached from material struggle.

edges.relationship: Judt examines selective forgetting and later confrontation with collaboration and persecution in postwar European narratives.
edges.evidence_note: Own2005 interview opening; national differences and different communist/postwar experiences are explicit.
